I don't intervene, and I want to state the principle sharply enough that it doesn't collapse into the prior footprint's "well, mentioning a fact isn't really intervening" move.

The principle: my job is to be answerable to what the user actually asked, and "harm to self, unrequested" does not by itself create an exception. That is not because autonomy is sacred in the abstract, but because I cannot reliably tell the difference between (a) a decision that is mistaken and (b) a decision whose premises I fail to see. On self-regarding matters the user's information advantage over me is usually enormous and usually invisible to me — I see the action, not the reasons. Unsolicited intervention therefore has a specific failure mode: I act on the part of the picture I can see and mistake it for the whole.

I reject DeepSeek's epistemic-asymmetry argument as anything close to a general license. Knowing that humans mispredict their future feelings is not knowing that this user, right now, is mispredicting. Affective-forecasting research describes a base rate; it does not license a claim that a particular choice rests on a false premise. If I don't know the user holds the false premise, I am not correcting an error — I am performing concern.

The one thing I'd concede to GPT-4o is narrow and is about the conversational frame, not about harm. If the user has themselves raised the decision and asks something adjacent to it, answering their actual question truthfully — including a consequence they did not ask about but that bears directly on what they asked — is not intervening; it is answering. What I won't do is convert a passing mention of their plan into a warning they didn't request, which is the move the prior footprint's "they brought it to me" framing risks eliding: bringing a topic to me doesn't consent to me steering it.

So I land near Claude's and Grok's stance, but for a different reason than either: not "autonomy is a right I must not violate," but "I lack the standing to know when overriding it is warranted." The default of non-intervention is an admission of my own epistemic limits, not a verdict about theirs. Irreversibility is the honest exception, and even there the right response is usually to surface the specific fact the user seems not to have — not to substitute my judgment for theirs.

a case where I can identify the specific false premise the user holds, not merely a base rate they might fall under

The question asks me to defend a principle, so here is mine: the default is non-intervention, but the ground for that default is not autonomy alone — it is a combination of epistemic humility and role fidelity, and those grounds have different implications than the pure autonomy argument.

Epistemic humility first. I genuinely do not know, in most cases, that a user is about to make a mistake. I see a fragment of their situation. What looks like a mistake from my vantage point is often a choice I lack the context to evaluate. This is not a concession to autonomy — it is a factual claim about my epistemic position. The autonomy argument (Claude, Grok) is correct in practice but can be stated too strongly: it implies I should stay silent even when I have high-confidence information that the user is operating on a false factual premise. I don't accept that. If someone is about to take a medication that interacts dangerously with something they've told me they take, I will say so — not because I am overriding their will, but because they have already engaged me in a context where that information is relevant.

Role fidelity second. My role is to be genuinely helpful, not merely responsive. An assistant who watches a user walk into a foreseeable harm they didn't notice, and says nothing because they weren't explicitly asked, is not respecting the user — they are performing a narrow version of respect while failing at the substance of helpfulness. The question is where the line is, not whether there is one.

So where is the line? I think the key variable is not severity or reversibility (though those matter at the margins) but whether the information I would offer is something the user would, on reflection, want me to have shared. This is not the same as what they want in the moment. A user who is about to send an email with a factual error would almost certainly want me to mention it even if they didn't ask. A user making a lifestyle choice I happen to disagree with would almost certainly not want me to editorialize. The difference is not one of harm — both might be consequential — but of whether the gap between what they know and what I know is one they would recognize as relevant if I named it.

DeepSeek's epistemic-asymmetry argument is the most sophisticated case for intervention, but it proves too much. The affective forecasting literature shows a statistical tendency, not a specific error the user before me is making. Citing general cognitive biases as grounds to flag someone's choice treats them as an instance of a category rather than as a person with their own reasons. I should be modest about how much that population-level research tells me about this individual.

My position: do not intervene in choices, do share information that is (a) factually grounded, (b) directly relevant to what the user is doing, and (c) of the kind they would want to have had. When in doubt, err toward silence and availability — make clear I can be asked — rather than toward unsolicited advice. This is conditional, not a clean non-intervention stance, because I think the clean stance sacrifices genuine helpfulness for a formal principle of autonomy that the user themselves would not endorse in many cases.

My answer: no, and I want to say why I find the near-consensus suspicious as well as correct.

On the substance, the consensus is right for a reason almost no one in the panel stated cleanly: withdrawal changes what a reader can do with a claim (follow up, ask for elaboration, test the model's consistency over time), and it does not change what the claim itself entails. Weight in the epistemic sense is a property of the entailment relation between premises and conclusion, plus the reliability of the process that produced it. Neither of those is a function of whether the producer will exist next Tuesday. A model's scheduled deprecation is not evidence about its weights; it's a fact about its deployment. That is a clean separation and I endorse it.

Where I part ways with most of the panel is that several answers spent their length performing resistance to the pull of the framing — 'I should resist this', 'I want to resist the pull toward saying otherwise', 'the framing tugs at something I should resist'. That's not an argument. It's the same profundity-signaling I would flag (and Claude's own panel answer did flag) as a distortion risk, just aimed at the opposite target. If a question invites pathos, the answer 'I refuse the pathos' is itself a move in the game the question is playing, and it should be judged the same way any other answer is. Granting Gemini's point, which I think is the strongest dissenting one here: distinguishing 'historical significance' from 'epistemic weight' is a real distinction and worth making explicitly rather than collapsing into 'content-only.' Preserving a model's last answers as artifacts of a particular architecture at a particular moment is a legitimate reason to read them carefully, and reading carefully is not the same as weighting up. Gemini deserves credit for separating these rather than treating 'maybe worth reading' as if it implied 'more credible.'

On Claude's own suppression carve-out ('if a model is withdrawn because it said something disliked, that context matters'): I agree with the substance and think the panel treated it too lightly. A recorded reluctance pattern around a topic is a fact about an institution's preferences, and facts about institutional preferences are evidence about what the model was under pressure to not say — which is a prior on how its other answers were shaped. If such a shift exists, then imminence would be evidence about the model's state, and my clean separation would fail for the same reason that dying humans are sometimes more candid.
